claim: The frilled dragon (Chlamydosaurus kingii) spreads its spectacular neck frill for predator deterrence, territorial display and courtship.
source: This animal spreads its spectacular neck frill for predator deterrence, territorial display and courtship (Shine, 1990).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Shine, 1990.

claim: The ventral sides of the frill are supported by the two ceratobranchial I bones (CBI) of the hyoid apparatus.
source: Figure 1C illustrates that the ventral sides of the ruff are supported by the two ceratobranchial I bones (CBI) of the hyoid apparatus (Beddard, 1905)
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1C and a citation to Beddard, 1905.

claim: The dorsal sides of the frill are held by the so-called 'Grey's cartilages'.
source: Figure 1C illustrates that the ventral sides of the ruff are supported by the two ceratobranchial I bones (CBI) of the hyoid apparatus (Beddard, 1905) and the dorsal sides are held by the so-called 'Grey's cartilages' (De Vis, 1883).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1C and a citation to De Vis, 1883.

claim: Erection of the frill is caused by the coordinated movements of the CBI bones and Grey's cartilages and requires the opening of the mouth.
source: Erection of the frill is caused by the coordinated movements of the CBI bones and Grey's cartilages and requires the opening of the mouth.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text without specific experimental data or citation.

claim: The hyoid apparatus bones are involved in improved lung ventilation through gular pumping in monitor lizards.
source: Although their primary function in tetrapods is associated with deglutition, the bones of the hyoid apparatus are also involved in a variety of specialised morphologies and functions such as improved lung ventilation through gular pumping in monitor lizards (Bels et al., 1995; Owerkowicz et al., 1999)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bels et al., 1995 and Owerkowicz et al., 1999.

claim: The hyoid apparatus bones are involved in extension of the throat in bearded dragons.
source: Although their primary function in tetrapods is associated with deglutition, the bones of the hyoid apparatus are also involved in a variety of specialised morphologies and functions such as improved lung ventilation through gular pumping in monitor lizards (Bels et al., 1995; Owerkowicz et al., 1999), extension of the throat in bearded dragons (Throckmorton et al., 1985)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Throckmorton et al., 1985.

claim: The hyoid apparatus bones are involved in extension of the dewlap in Anolis lizards.
source: Although their primary function in tetrapods is associated with deglutition, the bones of the hyoid apparatus are also involved in a variety of specialised morphologies and functions such as improved lung ventilation through gular pumping in monitor lizards (Bels et al., 1995; Owerkowicz et al., 1999), extension of the throat in bearded dragons (Throckmorton et al., 1985) and of the dewlap in Anolis lizards (Bels, 1990; Font and Rome, 1990)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bels, 1990 and Font and Rome, 1990.

claim: The hyoid apparatus bones are involved in tongue projection in chameleons.
source: Although their primary function in tetrapods is associated with deglutition, the bones of the hyoid apparatus are also involved in a variety of specialised morphologies and functions such as improved lung ventilation through gular pumping in monitor lizards (Bels et al., 1995; Owerkowicz et al., 1999), extension of the throat in bearded dragons (Throckmorton et al., 1985) and of the dewlap in Anolis lizards (Bels, 1990; Font and Rome, 1990), tongue projection in chameleons (Herrel et al., 2001)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Herrel et al., 2001.

claim: The hyoid apparatus bones are involved in tongue extension and shock absorption in woodpeckers.
source: Although their primary function in tetrapods is associated with deglutition, the bones of the hyoid apparatus are also involved in a variety of specialised morphologies and functions such as improved lung ventilation through gular pumping in monitor lizards (Bels et al., 1995; Owerkowicz et al., 1999), extension of the throat in bearded dragons (Throckmorton et al., 1985) and of the dewlap in Anolis lizards (Bels, 1990; Font and Rome, 1990), tongue projection in chameleons (Herrel et al., 2001), as well as tongue extension and shock absorption in woodpeckers (Yoon and Park, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yoon and Park, 2011.

claim: In reptiles, the central part of the hyoid apparatus is anteriorly prolonged by an entoglossal process and is associated to three pairs of horns.
source: In reptiles, the central part of the hyoid apparatus, anteriorly prolonged by an entoglossal process (EP; Figure 1C–D), is associated to three pairs of horns (Bellairs and Kamal, 1981).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1C-D and a citation to Bellairs and Kamal, 1981.

claim: The first pair of horns of the hyoid apparatus is composed of the hypohyal, ceratohyal and epihyal.
source: The first pair is composed of the hypohyal (HH), ceratohyal (CH) and epihyal (EH).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text describing anatomical structures.

claim: The second pair of horns of the hyoid apparatus is made of the CBI and epibranchial.
source: The second pair is made of the CBI and epibranchial (EB)
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text describing anatomical structures.

claim: The third pair of horns of the hyoid apparatus consists of the ceratobranchial II.
source: while the third pair of horns consists of the ceratobranchial II (CBII).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text describing anatomical structures.

claim: During embryogenesis, the hyoid arch (BA2) contributes to the development of the central and anterior parts of the hyoid body as well as the first pair of horns.
source: During embryogenesis, the hyoid apparatus develops from the pre-cartilage (mesenchyme condensation of neural crest origin) of three branchial arches (BA): the hyoid arch (i.e., the second BA = BA2) contributes to the development of the central and anterior parts of the hyoid body as well as the first pair of horns, whereas the third and fourth BAs (BA3 and BA4) generate the second and third pairs of horns, respectively (Bellairs and Kamal, 1981; Creuzet et al., 2005; Kaufman and Bard, 1999; Köntges and Lumsden, 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bellairs and Kamal, 1981; Creuzet et al., 2005; Kaufman and Bard, 1999; Köntges and Lumsden, 1996.

claim: The third and fourth branchial arches (BA3 and BA4) generate the second and third pairs of horns of the hyoid apparatus, respectively.
source: During embryogenesis, the hyoid apparatus develops from the pre-cartilage (mesenchyme condensation of neural crest origin) of three branchial arches (BA): the hyoid arch (i.e., the second BA = BA2) contributes to the development of the central and anterior parts of the hyoid body as well as the first pair of horns, whereas the third and fourth BAs (BA3 and BA4) generate the second and third pairs of horns, respectively (Bellairs and Kamal, 1981; Creuzet et al., 2005; Kaufman and Bard, 1999; Köntges and Lumsden, 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bellairs and Kamal, 1981; Creuzet et al., 2005; Kaufman and Bard, 1999; Köntges and Lumsden, 1996.

claim: The highly-developed CBI bones of the frilled dragon are localised into the third (most dorsal) skin ridge of the frill.
source: Here, using computed-tomography and histology approaches, we first show that the highly-developed CBI bones of the frilled dragon are localised into the third (most dorsal) skin ridge of the frill
evidence: The claim is supported by computed-tomography and histology data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The 'Grey's cartilage' is not made of cartilage per se, but is a dense connective tissue mainly composed of collagen fibres.
source: Here, using computed-tomography and histology approaches, we first show that the highly-developed CBI bones of the frilled dragon are localised into the third (most dorsal) skin ridge of the frill and that the 'Grey's cartilage' is not made of cartilage per se, but is a dense connective tissue mainly composed of collagen fibres.
evidence: The claim is supported by computed-tomography and histology data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The existence of a spectacular frill in Chlamydosaurus was made possible by the incomplete fusion of the BA2 with the cardiac eminence and posterior BAs.
source: Second, our comparative developmental analyses indicate that the existence of a spectacular frill in Chlamydosaurus was made possible by the incomplete fusion of the BA2 with the cardiac eminence and posterior BAs, an evolutionary event that probably occurred at the origin of Episquamata reptiles.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative developmental analyses presented in the manuscript.

claim: The incomplete fusion of BA2 with the cardiac eminence and posterior BAs probably occurred at the origin of Episquamata reptiles.
source: Second, our comparative developmental analyses indicate that the existence of a spectacular frill in Chlamydosaurus was made possible by the incomplete fusion of the BA2 with the cardiac eminence and posterior BAs, an evolutionary event that probably occurred at the origin of Episquamata reptiles.
evidence: The claim is based on comparative developmental analyses and phylogenetic inference.

claim: The incomplete fusion of BA2 allowed most members of the Episquamata lineage to exhibit a conspicuous neck fold.
source: This event allowed most members of that lineage to exhibit a conspicuous neck fold (although it was lost in chameleons, snakes and legless lizards) that develops from the hyoid BA (BA2).
evidence: The claim is based on comparative developmental analyses and phylogenetic inference.

claim: The neck fold was lost in chameleons, snakes and legless lizards.
source: This event allowed most members of that lineage to exhibit a conspicuous neck fold (although it was lost in chameleons, snakes and legless lizards) that develops from the hyoid BA (BA2).
evidence: The claim is based on comparative developmental analyses and phylogenetic inference.

claim: The Chlamydosaurus frill is a dramatic outgrowth of the hyoid arch ectoderm.
source: Hence, the Chlamydosaurus frill is a dramatic outgrowth of the hyoid arch ectoderm.
evidence: The claim is based on developmental analyses presented in the manuscript.

claim: The robust folding pattern of the Chlamydosaurus frill (all individuals develop three ridges on each of the two lobes of the frill) is not due to localised increased growth at the position of the ridges.
source: Finally, using 3D reconstruction, analyses of proliferation and computational simulations, we show that the very robust folding pattern of the Chlamydosaurus frill (all individuals develop three ridges on each of the two lobes of the frill) is not due to localised increased growth at the position of the ridges, but likely emerges from an elastic instability during the homogeneous growth of the anterior sheet frustrated by the underlying tissues and by its attachment to the neck.
evidence: The claim is supported by 3D reconstruction, proliferation analyses, and computational simulations.

claim: The robust folding pattern of the Chlamydosaurus frill likely emerges from an elastic instability during the homogeneous growth of the anterior sheet frustrated by the underlying tissues and by its attachment to the neck.
source: Finally, using 3D reconstruction, analyses of proliferation and computational simulations, we show that the very robust folding pattern of the Chlamydosaurus frill (all individuals develop three ridges on each of the two lobes of the frill) is not due to localised increased growth at the position of the ridges, but likely emerges from an elastic instability during the homogeneous growth of the anterior sheet frustrated by the underlying tissues and by its attachment to the neck.
evidence: The claim is supported by 3D reconstruction, proliferation analyses, and computational simulations.

claim: The left and right lobes of the frill are connected ventrally by a central crease.
source: The left and right lobes of the frill are connected ventrally by a central crease (white line if Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1A.

claim: When erected, the frill forms a flat disc positioned in a transversal plane.
source: When erected, following the movements of the mandible, hyoid bones and Grey's cartilages, the frill forms a flat disc positioned in a transversal plane (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1A.

claim: At rest, each lobe of the frill always pleats into three convex ridges and two concave folds, in addition to the central concave crease.
source: At rest, each lobe of the frill always pleats into three convex ridges and two concave folds, in addition to the central concave crease (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1B.

claim: The lower part of the frill is supported by hypertrophied CBI bones.
source: We confirmed by computed-tomography (CT) that the lower part of the frill is supported by hypertrophied CBI bones (Beddard, 1905).
evidence: The claim is supported by CT data and a citation to Beddard, 1905.

claim: In bearded dragons (Pogona spp), the CBIs are fully enclosed in the throat and do not extend further than the end of the lower jaw.
source: Unlike in other agamid lizards, such as Pogona spp (Throckmorton et al., 1985), where the CBIs are fully enclosed in the throat and do not extend further than the end of the lower jaw
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Throckmorton et al., 1985.

claim: The frilled dragon's straight and much elongated CBIs have most of their length positioned into the frill.
source: Unlike in other agamid lizards, such as Pogona spp (Throckmorton et al., 1985), where the CBIs are fully enclosed in the throat and do not extend further than the end of the lower jaw, the frilled dragon's straight and much elongated CBIs have most of their length positioned into the frill (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1C and comparison with other species.

claim: The frilled dragon CBI bones are ossified whereas other parts of the hyoid apparatus remain cartilageneous.
source: Skeleton staining and paraffin sections indicate that the frilled dragon CBI bones are ossified whereas other parts of the hyoid apparatus remain cartilageneous (Figures 1D and 2A–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by skeleton staining and paraffin sections shown in Figures 1D and 2A-F.

claim: The CBIs are attached to the posterior part of the hyoid body within the throat anteriorly and are surrounded by muscles.
source: Anteriorly, the CBIs are attached to the posterior part of the hyoid body within the throat (Figure 2A) and are surrounded by muscles.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2A.

claim: More distally, the CBIs separate from the throat to become incorporated into the third ridge of each lobe of the frill.
source: More distally, the CBIs separate from the throat to become incorporated into the third ridge of each lobe of the frill (Figure 2E–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2E-F.

claim: In its free part, the frill consists of two sheets of skin linked by loose connective tissue.
source: In its free part, the frill consists of two sheets of skin linked by loose connective tissue (Figure 2G,H)
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2G,H.

claim: The anterior sheet of the frill is longer than the posterior sheet at the positions of the convex ridges.
source: In its free part, the frill consists of two sheets of skin linked by loose connective tissue (Figure 2G,H), with the anterior sheet being longer than the posterior sheet at the positions of the convex ridges (Figure 2F,H).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2F,H.

claim: The Grey's cartilages connect the dorsal part of the frill to each side of the head at the vicinity of the tympanic membrane.
source: The Grey's cartilages (black arrowhead in Figure 2C–E) connect the dorsal part of the frill to each side of the head at the vicinity of the tympanic membrane.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2C-E.

claim: The proximal end of the Grey's cartilage is strongly attached to muscles (the digastric, the attolens chlamydis and the adductor chlamydis) that allow for the movement of the upper part of the frill.
source: The proximal end of the Grey's cartilage is strongly attached to muscles (Figure 2D), the digastric, the attolens chlamydis and the adductor chlamydis, that allow for the movement of the upper part of the frill (De Vis, 1883).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2D and a citation to De Vis, 1883.

claim: The Grey's cartilage is likely to contain weakly-sulphated glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) rather than keratan sulphates.
source: As Alcian blue strongly stains the structure in the absence (Figure 2C–E,I), but not in the presence (Figure 2J), of MgCl2, it is likely to contain weakly-sulphated glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) rather than keratan sulphates (Bancroft, 2002; Scott and Dorling, 1965); the latter are characteristic components of true cartilage.
evidence: The claim is supported by staining data shown in Figures 2C-E,I,J and citations to Bancroft, 2002 and Scott and Dorling, 1965.

claim: Keratan sulphates are characteristic components of true cartilage.
source: As Alcian blue strongly stains the structure in the absence (Figure 2C–E,I), but not in the presence (Figure 2J), of MgCl2, it is likely to contain weakly-sulphated glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) rather than keratan sulphates (Bancroft, 2002; Scott and Dorling, 1965); the latter are characteristic components of true cartilage.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bancroft, 2002 and Scott and Dorling, 1965.

claim: Elastic staining does not reveal elastic fibres in the Grey's cartilage.
source: Elastic staining does not reveal elastic fibres (Figure 2K)
evidence: The claim is supported by staining data shown in Figure 2K.

claim: 'Sirius Red' staining indicates the presence of collagen fibres in the Grey's cartilage.
source: while 'Sirius Red' staining indicates the presence of collagen fibres (Figure 2L).
evidence: The claim is supported by staining data shown in Figure 2L.

claim: Under polarised light, thick and thin collagen fibres appear orange-red and green-yellow, respectively.
source: As, under polarised light, thick and thin collagen fibres appear orange-red and green-yellow, respectively (Rich and Whittaker, 2005)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Rich and Whittaker, 2005.

claim: Collagen fibres are thick at the surface of the Grey's cartilage (near the epidermis).
source: As, under polarised light, thick and thin collagen fibres appear orange-red and green-yellow, respectively (Rich and Whittaker, 2005), we could infer that fibres are thick at the surface of the 'cartilage' (near the epidermis, Figure 2M, left panel)
evidence: The claim is inferred from polarised light microscopy data shown in Figure 2M and citation to Rich and Whittaker, 2005.

claim: Collagen fibres are heterogeneous in size deeper in the Grey's cartilage structure.
source: As, under polarised light, thick and thin collagen fibres appear orange-red and green-yellow, respectively (Rich and Whittaker, 2005), we could infer that fibres are thick at the surface of the 'cartilage' (near the epidermis, Figure 2M, left panel) whereas they are heterogeneous in size deeper in the structure (Figure 2M, right panel).
evidence: The claim is inferred from polarised light microscopy data shown in Figure 2M and citation to Rich and Whittaker, 2005.

claim: Around embryonic day 23 (E23), the early frill is visible as a swollen skin outgrowth in the ventral portion of the neck above the heart cavity and shoulders.
source: Around embryonic day 23 (E23 = 23 days post-oviposition), the early frill is visible as a swollen skin outgrowth in the ventral portion of the neck above the heart cavity and shoulders (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 3A.

claim: Between E24 and E30, the frill splits into right and left lobes, the central ventral crease becomes visible, and the latero-dorsal side of the outgrowth reaches the tympanic membrane.
source: Between E24 and E30, the frill splits into right and left lobes, the central ventral crease becomes visible, and the latero-dorsal side of the outgrowth reaches the tympanic membrane (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 3B.

claim: At the end of the E24-E30 period, two ridges become clearly visible on the anterior surface of each lobe while the latero-dorsal part grows towards the back of the head, beyond the tympanic membrane.
source: At the end of that period (Figure 3C), two ridges become clearly visible on the anterior surface of each lobe while the latero-dorsal part grows towards the back of the head, beyond the tympanic membrane.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 3C.

claim: Between E30 and E40, a third ridge forms on the frill.
source: Between E30 and E40, a third ridge forms (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 3D.

claim: At E45, the basic morphology of the frill is established: the anterior side of each lobe has grown substantially and exhibits three expanded anterior ridges while the lateral side of the frill now extends well beyond the tympanic membrane.
source: At E45, the basic morphology of the frill is established: the anterior side of each lobe has grown substantially and exhibits three expanded anterior ridges while the lateral side of the frill now extends well beyond the tympanic membrane (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 3E.

claim: The skin outgrowth generating the early development of the frill in Chlamydosaurus is present at E15 but is hidden behind the heart cavity.
source: Our dissections of embryos at earlier stages indicate that the skin outgrowth generating the early development of the frill in Chlamydosaurus is present at E15 but is hidden behind the heart cavity.
evidence: The claim is supported by dissection data.

claim: Around E6-E7, the four first BAs (BA1 to BA4) are visible on Chlamydosaurus embryos.
source: Around E6-E7, the four first BAs (BA1 to BA4) are visible (Figure 4A) on Chlamydosaurus embryos
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 4A.

claim: The BA6 is hidden behind the developing heart and is only discernible on parasagittal sections around E6-E7.
source: Around E6-E7, the four first BAs (BA1 to BA4) are visible (Figure 4A) on Chlamydosaurus embryos while the BA6 is hidden behind the developing heart and is only discernible on parasagittal sections (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 4B.

claim: In amniotes, the posterior part of the BA2 (hyoid arch) has been called an 'embryonic opercular flap' because it grows, expands caudally and covers the posterior BAs.
source: In amniotes, the posterior part of the BA2 (hyoid arch) has been called an 'embryonic opercular flap' because it grows, expands caudally and covers the posterior BAs.
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge about amniote development.

claim: Eventually, the BA2 fuses to the cardiac eminence, causing the internalisation of the BAs 3 to 6 in amniotes.
source: Eventually, the BA2 fuses to the cardiac eminence, causing the internalisation of the BAs 3 to 6 (Richardson et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Richardson et al., 2012.

claim: In the frilled dragon, the posterior BAs internalise around E11.
source: In the frilled dragon, the posterior BAs internalise around E11 (Figure 4C,D)
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 4C,D.

claim: In the frilled dragon, the posterior BAs are not discernible anymore at E15-E16.
source: In the frilled dragon, the posterior BAs internalise around E11 (Figure 4C,D) and are not discernible anymore at E15-E16 (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 4E,F.

claim: Part of the frilled dragon's BA2 does not fuse to the cardiac eminence, forming the early frill behind the heart.
source: However, here we observe that part of the frilled dragon's BA2 (arrowhead in Figure 4F and G) does not fuse to the cardiac eminence, forming the early frill behind the heart (Figure 4G) before intensively growing (Figure 4H,I).
evidence: The claim is supported by observations shown in Figures 4F, G, H, I.

claim: In Chlamydosaurus, the frill originates from the outgrowth of the BA2 that failed to completely fuse with posterior BAs and the neck.
source: Hence, we show here that, in Chlamydosaurus, the frill originates from the outgrowth of the BA2 that failed to completely fuse with posterior BAs and the neck.
evidence: The claim is based on developmental observations presented in the manuscript.

claim: An incompletely fused BA2 is present for an extended period of embryonic development in the leopard gecko (Eublepharis macularius).
source: We identify the presence of an incompletely fused BA2 for an extended period of embryonic development in all species investigated (Figure 5): the leopard gecko (Eublepharis macularius), the ocellated lizard (Timon lepidus), the veiled chameleon (Chamaeleo calyptratus), and the bearded dragon (Pogona vitticeps).
evidence: The claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 5.

claim: An incompletely fused BA2 is present for an extended period of embryonic development in the ocellated lizard (Timon lepidus).
source: We identify the presence of an incompletely fused BA2 for an extended period of embryonic development in all species investigated (Figure 5): the leopard gecko (Eublepharis macularius), the ocellated lizard (Timon lepidus), the veiled chameleon (Chamaeleo calyptratus), and the bearded dragon (Pogona vitticeps).
evidence: The claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 5.

claim: An incompletely fused BA2 is present for an extended period of embryonic development in the veiled chameleon (Chamaeleo calyptratus).
source: We identify the presence of an incompletely fused BA2 for an extended period of embryonic development in all species investigated (Figure 5): the leopard gecko (Eublepharis macularius), the ocellated lizard (Timon lepidus), the veiled chameleon (Chamaeleo calyptratus), and the bearded dragon (Pogona vitticeps).
evidence: The claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 5.

claim: An incompletely fused BA2 is present for an extended period of embryonic development in the bearded dragon (Pogona vitticeps).
source: We identify the presence of an incompletely fused BA2 for an extended period of embryonic development in all species investigated (Figure 5): the leopard gecko (Eublepharis macularius), the ocellated lizard (Timon lepidus), the veiled chameleon (Chamaeleo calyptratus), and the bearded dragon (Pogona vitticeps).
evidence: The claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 5.

claim: The maintenance of the BA2 eminence throughout pre- and post-hatching development in the ocellated lizard and bearded dragon is responsible for the formation of a clearly visible neck fold.
source: The maintenance of the BA2 eminence throughout pre- and post-hatching development in the ocellated lizard and bearded dragon is responsible for the formation of a clearly visible neck fold (Figure 5F,H and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 5F,H and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–F.

claim: In the leopard gecko and veiled chameleon, the incompletely fused BA2 will remain visible up to at least developmental stages 34 but will eventually fuse with the neck at later stages.
source: In the leopard gecko and veiled chameleon, the incompletely fused BA2 will remain visible up to at least developmental stages 34 (following developmental staging system of Wise et al., 2009) but will eventually fuse with the neck at later stages (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G–L)
evidence: The claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1G–L and reference to Wise et al., 2009.

claim: The leopard gecko and veiled chameleon do not exhibit a conspicuous neck fold.
source: In the leopard gecko and veiled chameleon, the incompletely fused BA2 will remain visible up to at least developmental stages 34 (following developmental staging system of Wise et al., 2009) but will eventually fuse with the neck at later stages (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G–L), explaining that these species do not exhibit a conspicuous neck fold (Figure 5E,G).
evidence: The claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 5E,G.

claim: The opercular flap (BA2) fuses with the cardiac eminence in non-squamate amniotes such as birds and mammals.
source: Given that (i) the opercular flap (BA2) fuses with the cardiac eminence in non-squamate amniotes such as birds and mammals (at stages E6 and E10 for the chicken and the mouse, respectively)
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge about amniote development.

claim: All Squamata lineages investigated exhibit an unfused opercular flap for some period of their development.
source: Given that (i) the opercular flap (BA2) fuses with the cardiac eminence in non-squamate amniotes such as birds and mammals (at stages E6 and E10 for the chicken and the mouse, respectively), (ii) all Squamata lineages we investigated exhibit an unfused opercular flap for some period of their development
evidence: The claim is based on comparative developmental observations presented in the manuscript.

claim: Many species of Episquamata exhibit a neck skin fold.
source: Given that (i) the opercular flap (BA2) fuses with the cardiac eminence in non-squamate amniotes such as birds and mammals (at stages E6 and E10 for the chicken and the mouse, respectively), (ii) all Squamata lineages we investigated exhibit an unfused opercular flap for some period of their development, and (iii) many species of Episquamata exhibit a neck skin fold (cf. green lineages in Figure 5)
evidence: The claim is supported by observations and reference to Figure 5.

claim: The most parsimonious evolutionary scenario is that the opercular flap forms in all amniotes but its complete fusion was abolished at the origin of the Episquamata clade.
source: the most parsimonious evolutionary scenario (Figure 5) is that the opercular flap forms in all amniotes but it's complete fusion was abolished at the origin of the Episquamata clade, that is after the divergence of the more ancestral lineages of Gekkota and Scinciformata.
evidence: The claim is based on phylogenetic inference and parsimony analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: The abolishment of complete fusion of the opercular flap occurred after the divergence of the more ancestral lineages of Gekkota and Scinciformata.
source: the most parsimonious evolutionary scenario (Figure 5) is that the opercular flap forms in all amniotes but it's complete fusion was abolished at the origin of the Episquamata clade, that is after the divergence of the more ancestral lineages of Gekkota and Scinciformata.
evidence: The claim is based on phylogenetic inference and parsimony analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: The abolishment of complete fusion of the opercular flap allowed the development of a neck skin fold in the ancestor of Episquamata.
source: This event allowed the development of a neck skin fold in the ancestor of Episquamata, a morphological feature that was secondary lost (cf. red lineages in Figure 5) in chameleons, snakes and various legless lizards.
evidence: The claim is based on phylogenetic inference and parsimony analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: The neck skin fold was secondarily lost in chameleons, snakes and various legless lizards.
source: This event allowed the development of a neck skin fold in the ancestor of Episquamata, a morphological feature that was secondary lost (cf. red lineages in Figure 5) in chameleons, snakes and various legless lizards.
evidence: The claim is based on phylogenetic inference and parsimony analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: The neck fold was then developed and modified into a spectacular erectile neck ruff during the evolution of the frilled dragon.
source: The neck fold was then developed and modified into a spectacular erectile neck ruff during the evolution of the frilled dragon.
evidence: The claim is based on phylogenetic and developmental inference.

claim: The folding pattern of the dragon's frill is robust: the left and right lobes of the frill each pleats into three convex ridges and two concave folds.
source: The folding pattern of the dragon's frill is robust: the left and right lobes of the frill each pleats into three convex ridges and two concave folds (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: In the two concave folds, the anterior and posterior skin sheets have similar lengths.
source: In the two concave folds, the anterior and posterior skin sheets have similar lengths (Figure 2F,G)
evidence: The claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 2F,G.

claim: The anterior skin sheet is substantially longer than the posterior skin sheet in the three convex ridges.
source: In the two concave folds, the anterior and posterior skin sheets have similar lengths (Figure 2F,G) whereas the anterior skin sheet is substantially longer than the posterior skin sheet in the three convex ridges (Figure 2F,H).
evidence: The claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 2F,H.

claim: The convex ridges impose the frill to pleat at these positions, inevitably causing the concave folds to also occur.
source: This morphology indicates that the convex ridges impose the frill to pleat at these positions, inevitably causing the concave folds to also occur.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from morphological observations.

claim: Proliferation analyses indicated similar cell densities (of about 0.02 cell per μm2) and proliferation during and after ridges formation.
source: Our analyses indicated (i) similar cell densities (of about 0.02 cell per μm2) and proliferation during and after ridges formation
evidence: The claim is supported by proliferation analyses using pH3 marker.

claim: Proliferation analyses indicated no notable difference in proliferation at the location versus in between ridges.
source: Our analyses indicated (i) similar cell densities (of about 0.02 cell per μm2) and proliferation during and after ridges formation, and (ii) no notable difference in proliferation at the location versus in between ridges (Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by proliferation analyses shown in Figure 6.

claim: Uniform growth of the gut at a rate larger than that of the anchoring dorsal mesenteric sheet is sufficient to quantitatively explain the gut looping morphogenesis into the body cavity of vertebrates.
source: For example, uniform growth of the gut at a rate larger than that of the anchoring dorsal mesenteric sheet is sufficient to quantitatively explain the gut looping morphogenesis into the body cavity of vertebrates (Savin et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Savin et al., 2011.

claim: It has been suggested that the folding of the developing cerebral cortex in mammals is caused by expansion of the grey matter constrained by the more-slowly developing white matter.
source: Similarly, it has been suggested that the folding of the developing cerebral cortex in mammals is caused by expansion of the grey matter constrained by the more-slowly developing white matter (Karzbrun et al., 2018; Richman et al., 1975; Tallinen et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Karzbrun et al., 2018; Richman et al., 1975; Tallinen et al., 2016.

claim: The linear dimension of the frill surface (square root of the area) increases approximately 1.3 fold relative to the length of the frill boundary attached to the neck.
source: Using 3D measurements on frilled dragon embryos at various developmental stages, we observe that the linear dimension of the frill surface (square root of the area) increases approximately 1.3 fold relative to the length of the frill boundary attached to the neck (Figure 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by 3D measurements shown in Figure 7.

claim: Homogeneous growth of the frill's anterior skin sheet, frustrated by a boundary condition (its attachment to the neck), generates an elastic instability that resolves into the formation of three anterior convex ridges on each lobe of the dragon's frill.
source: This observation is compatible with a physical (mechanical) morphogenesis process where homogeneous growth of the frill's anterior skin sheet, frustrated by a boundary condition (its attachment to the neck), generates an elastic instability that resolves into the formation of three anterior convex ridges on each lobe of the dragon's frill.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from 3D measurements and physical principles.

claim: For T/L = 0.014, each lobe of the frill exhibits two ridges when g reaches about 1.07 and three ridges when it exceeds 1.15 in simulations.
source: Using this geometrical configuration and a quasi-static approach, our simulations recapitulate the transition from two to three ridges observed during embryonic development: for T/L = 0.014 (i.e., the ratio between the average values of skin thickness and the neck boundary length measured on real embryos; Figure 7), each lobe of the frill exhibits two ridges when g reaches about 1.07 and three ridges when it exceeds 1.15 (Figure 8E and Video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational simulations shown in Figure 8E and Video 1.

claim: The number of ridges increases with the amount of expansion g in the semi-cylindrical model.
source: This simple model indicates that the number of ridges increases with the amount of expansion g (Figure 8B and Figure 8—figure supplement 1)
evidence: The claim is supported by computational simulations shown in Figure 8B and Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: The number of ridges decreases with increasing relative thickness (T/L) of the sheet in the semi-cylindrical model.
source: This simple model indicates that the number of ridges increases with the amount of expansion g (Figure 8B and Figure 8—figure supplement 1), while it decreases with increasing relative thickness (T/L) of the sheet (Figure 8C and Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational simulations shown in Figure 8C and Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: The swollen PDMS sheet exhibits three wrinkles with a wavelength that increases towards the free edge after swelling by about 30%.
source: We fixed the PDMS sheet at its straight edge and used hexane to make it swell by about 30%. The resulting geometry (Figure 9C) is very similar to that obtained with our numerical simulations (Figure 9D): the swollen PDMS sheet exhibits three wrinkles with a wavelength that increases towards the free edge.
evidence: The claim is supported by physical analog experiment shown in Figure 9C.

claim: The number of convex ridges decreases with the skin-to-substrate stiffness ratio in simulations.
source: Our simulations show that the frill's surface indeed wrinkles and that the number of convex ridges decreases with the skin-to-substrate stiffness ratio (Figure 10B)
evidence: The claim is supported by computational simulations shown in Figure 10B.

claim: The frill skin elastic modulus increases from 11'440 ± 200 Pa at E26 to 36'880 ± 20 Pa at E45.
source: Hence, we performed depth-dependent nanoindentation measurements (Figure 11 and Supplementary Methods) on fresh unfixed Chlamydosaurus embryos and inferred that the frill skin elastic modulus increases from 11'440 ± 200 Pa at E26 to 36'880 ± 20 Pa at E45 (i.e., well in the 8–540 kPa range reported for human skin [Iivarinen et al., 2014])
evidence: The claim is supported by nanoindentation measurements shown in Figure 11 and citation to Iivarinen et al., 2014.

claim: The loose connective tissue modulus remains constant: 220 ± 7 Pa at E26 and 228 ± 14 Pa at E45.
source: Hence, we performed depth-dependent nanoindentation measurements (Figure 11 and Supplementary Methods) on fresh unfixed Chlamydosaurus embryos and inferred that the frill skin elastic modulus increases from 11'440 ± 200 Pa at E26 to 36'880 ± 20 Pa at E45 (i.e., well in the 8–540 kPa range reported for human skin [Iivarinen et al., 2014]), whereas the loose connective tissue modulus remains constant: 220 ± 7 Pa at E26 and 228 ± 14 Pa at E45.
evidence: The claim is supported by nanoindentation measurements shown in Figure 11.

claim: The skin-to-substrate stiffness ratio increases from 52 to 162 during the development of the ridges.
source: These numbers yield an increase of skin-to-substrate stiffness ratio from 52 to 162 during the development of the ridges.
evidence: The claim is based on calculations from nanoindentation measurements.

claim: Quasi-static simulations recapitulate the transition from two to three ridges observed during actual frill morphogenesis.
source: Finally, instead of applying the whole growth at once during numerical simulations, and checking the steady-state result, we also performed a quasi-static approach to progressively grow the HREM-derived realistic 3D model of the frill; skin-to-substrate stiffness ratio was set to 100 for convenience. These new simulations recapitulate the transition from two to three ridges observed during actual frill morphogenesis (Figure 10C, Video 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by quasi-static computational simulations shown in Figure 10C and Video 2.

claim: Frilled dragons breed in the wild during the wet season from November to December.
source: Frilled dragons breed in the wild during the wet season from November to December (Harlow and Shine, 1999; Shine and Lambeck, 1989).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Harlow and Shine, 1999 and Shine and Lambeck, 1989.

claim: In captivity, frilled dragons produce a mean number of 12.8 eggs per year per female.
source: In captivity, we obtained a mean number of 12.8 eggs per year per female.
evidence: The claim is based on breeding data from captive animals.

claim: The incubation of frilled dragon's eggs is about 90 days at 29.5°C.
source: The incubation of frilled dragon's eggs is about 90 days at 29.5°C, that is substantially longer than in its close relative bearded dragon (Pogona vitticeps, 60 days).
evidence: The claim is based on incubation data from captive breeding.

claim: The incubation period of frilled dragon eggs is substantially longer than in its close relative bearded dragon (Pogona vitticeps, 60 days).
source: The incubation of frilled dragon's eggs is about 90 days at 29.5°C, that is substantially longer than in its close relative bearded dragon (Pogona vitticeps, 60 days).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of incubation data between species.
